metadata.description: How an A/B test can look significant and still be wrong: a real MSN carousel test that read as a significant loss was a win — a bot filter had removed the most engaged users from one group (a sample ratio mismatch). Plus peeking: checking daily makes a quarter of no-difference tests crown a winner. Built with real Python simulations.

beats.role_note: Manim — the stakes: a real MSN test that said 'don't ship'
beats.narration_text: Here's the problem. A product team at MSN gave a carousel sixteen rotating cards instead of twelve. They expected more clicks. The test said the opposite: a statistically significant drop. On that result, you don't ship. This is real, from a twenty nineteen paper led by Microsoft researchers.
beats.visual_intent: A carousel of 12 cards slides in, then grows to 16. An engagement arrow dives; 'significant drop · p < 0.05' beside it; verdict card 'Don't ship.' Source line 'Fabijan et al., KDD 2019 · MSN carousel'. Corner handle 'Supriya'.

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — cycle 1, the actual code: excerpt of py/carousel_v1.py (lines 10, 13–19, 26–29; verbatim, blank lines collapsed)
beats.narration_text: Here's the simulation. Most users click zero to six times. One and a half percent are fans, and the new carousel gives them forty more clicks. Then the standard cleanup: anyone over eighty clicks counts as a bot and gets dropped.

props.title: carousel_v1.py
props.code:
BOT = 80     # clicks: above = bot

def user(arm):
    if random() < 0.015:  # fan
        pre, up = 60, 40
    else:
        pre = randint(0, 6)
        up = random() < 0.2
    return pre, pre + arm * up

def keep(users):
    # drop "bots": too many clicks
    return [c for _, c in users
            if c <= BOT]

beats.role_note: Manim — cycle 1 output, the misleading readout (real py/carousel_v1.out)
beats.narration_text: The readout. Control: three point eight nine clicks per user. Test: three point two. A z score of minus forty. Significant, and clearly worse. Don't ship.
beats.visual_intent: Two bars grow: control 3.89, test 3.20 clicks per user, test bar sinking below; 'z −40.4 · p < 1e-9'; 'SIMULATION' tag; verdict 'Don't ship.' Corner handle 'Supriya'.

beats.narration_text: The revision. Before reading any metric, check the split. Fifty-fifty in should mean fifty-fifty out.

props.command: claude "before any metric: check the 50/50 split, then fix the bot filter"

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — cycle 2, the actual code: excerpt of py/carousel_v2.py (lines 28–32, 35–37, 41–42; verbatim, blank lines collapsed)
beats.narration_text: Two changes. A chi-square test on the group sizes against fifty-fifty. And the fix: judge bots by their clicks from before the test, which the new carousel can't touch.

props.title: carousel_v2.py
props.code:
def kept(users, col):
    # col 1 = clicks during test
    # col 0 = clicks before test
    return [u[1] for u in users
            if u[col] <= BOT]

nc = len(kept(ctrl, 1))
nt = len(kept(test, 1))
chi2, p = srm_check(nc, nt)

mc, mt, z, p = z_test(
    kept(ctrl, 0), kept(test, 0))

beats.role_note: Manim — cycle 2 output: SRM fires, then the flip (real py/carousel_v2.out) + Flag C source line
beats.narration_text: The test group is three thousand users short. The odds of that by chance: about two in a million. That's a sample ratio mismatch. Fix the filter, and it's three point eight nine against four point six five. The loss was a win.
beats.visual_intent: Two user stacks 200,000 vs 196,997; the gap highlighted '3,003 missing'; 'SRM p 2e-06'. Then B04's bars re-grow to 3.89 vs 4.65, test in terracotta, arrow flips up: 'The loss was a win.' Source line (Flag C): 'Real SRMs are this subtle — Fabijan et al.'s example: 821,588 vs 815,482 users, < 1 in 500k by chance.' Corner handle 'Supriya'.

beats.role_note: Manim — peeking, one beat (approved): real py/peeking.out curve + Johari et al. 2015
beats.narration_text: The second lie is peeking. I ran a thousand A-A tests, both groups identical, checking every day for twenty days. Stop at the first significant day, and a quarter of them crown a winner. Look once, at the end: under five percent. Researchers at Stanford and Optimizely found nonstop checking can push it past thirty.
beats.visual_intent: A day axis 1–20; the false-winner curve climbs from 3.5% to 24.6% against a dashed 5% line; 'look once: 3.8%' marker at day 20; '1,000 A/A tests · SIMULATION'. Then 'checking nonstop: > 30%' with source line 'Johari, Pekelis & Walsh, 2015'. Corner handle 'Supriya'.

beats.narration_text: Back to MSN. The bot filter had dropped the most engaged users in the sixteen-card group. Once that was fixed, the result flipped, and the feature shipped. The paper says about six percent of Microsoft's experiments show this mismatch. So: check the split first, fix your sample size in advance, and if you must peek, use a test built for it.
beats.visual_intent: The B01 carousel returns, arrow flips up, 'shipped'. '~6% of Microsoft experiments had an SRM' (Fabijan et al. 2019). Three numbered checks build in: 'Check the split first' · 'Fix the sample size in advance' · 'Must peek? Use a sequential test'. Corner handle 'Supriya'.
